title: Weaponizing the Bond: Pet Abuse as a Mediator of IPV Victimization and Mental Health Symptomology.
abstract: The purpose of the current study was to understand how the perpetration of pet abuse (i.e., dog and cat), in the context of intimate partner violence (IPV), contributes to victims' mental health outcomes. We were specifically interested in examining 1) the relationship between a partner's pet abuse perpetration and depression, anxiety, and PTSD and 2) how pet abuse might mediate the relationship between IPV victimization and mental health outcomes.Participants (= 1,173) were recruited online via TestSet and responded to items related to IPV victimization, their partner's maltreatment of dogs or cats, and current mental health symptomology. Separate path models estimated the direct and indirect effects of physical, psychological, and sexual IPV victimization on depression, anxiety, and PTSD symptoms, with a partner's cat and dog abuse specified as mediators.Psychological IPV victimization and pet abuse consistently emerged as the strongest direct predictors of mental health symptomology across all models. Dog and cat abuse significantly mediated the relationships between physical and sexual IPV, but not psychological IPV, on victims' depressive, anxiety, and PTSD symptoms.Pet abuse is a significant risk marker for IPV and psychological distress. Pet abuse warrants both legal recognition as a form of domestic violence and clinical recognition as a distinct source of trauma.
